what: Build Check Part 3 (the plain read, ROC Operations Manual §14.2A): a session that saw only Pip's statements read them as a gardener would, sentence by sentence. First read of version 0.1, second read of version 0.2.

statements.question: Which months do I prune my rose?
statements.text: In the UK, the main pruning is done in late winter or early spring, in February or March. Two rose growers say January or February, and one garden company says on a frost-free day between November and March. Months are only a guide, because frosts vary from year to year.
statements.shown_to: Gardeners in the United Kingdom only

statements.question: Which months do I prune my rose?
statements.text: In the south, prune around mid-February. In northern and colder areas, wait until March; one garden company says mid to late March. Months are only a guide, because frosts vary from year to year.
statements.shown_to: Gardeners in the United Kingdom only

statements.question: Which months do I prune my rose?
statements.text: In the Midlands and the south of England, one rose nursery says to do the main pruning in November or December. Others say February or March. Months are only a guide, because frosts vary from year to year.
statements.shown_to: Gardeners in the Midlands and the south of England only

statements.question: Which months do I prune my rose?
statements.text: In the north of England and Scotland, one rose nursery says to do the main pruning between January and late February. Others say to wait until March in northern and colder areas. Months are only a guide, because frosts vary from year to year.
statements.shown_to: Gardeners in the north of England or in Scotland only

statements.question: Which months do I prune my rose?
statements.text: Prune on a frost-free day, before new growth begins and the buds start to open. One source says to prune when growth is just resuming.
statements.shown_to: Gardeners in the United Kingdom only

statements.question: Which months do I prune my rose?
statements.text: Two rose growers say a rose can be trimmed in autumn, between September and November, so that winter wind does not rock or damage it. One of them says this is for tall roses, and that it is too early then for a hard prune. Months are only a guide.
statements.shown_to: Gardeners in the United Kingdom only

statements.question: Which months do I prune my rose?
statements.text: One rose grower says not to prune a rose hard in autumn, because frost can then damage the cut tips.
statements.shown_to: Gardeners in the United Kingdom only

statements.question: When do I start and stop feeding?
statements.text: Give the first feed in spring, in March or April, before the rose flowers. One rose grower says it can go on from the end of February. Months are only a guide.
statements.shown_to: Gardeners in the United Kingdom only

statements.question: When do I start and stop feeding?
statements.text: Feed the rose again in mid-summer, after its first flush of flowers. One rose grower says in July. Months are only a guide.
statements.shown_to: Gardeners in the United Kingdom only

statements.question: When do I start and stop feeding?
statements.text: One rose grower says to give the last feed before the end of August, so that the rose can slow down for winter and frost does not damage new growth. Months are only a guide, because frosts vary from year to year.
statements.shown_to: Gardeners in the United Kingdom only

statements.question: When do I stop deadheading?
statements.text: Deadhead (remove the faded flowers) while the rose is in flower, through summer and into autumn. One rose grower says to keep deadheading in October. Months are only a guide.
statements.shown_to: Gardeners in the United Kingdom only

statements.question: When do I stop deadheading?
statements.text: If your rose is grown for its hips (the rose's fruit), stop deadheading early so that the hips have time to form. One source says to stop in mid-summer, and one rose grower says after the second flush of flowers.
statements.shown_to: Gardeners in the United Kingdom only

statements.question: When do I stop deadheading?
statements.text: I couldn't find a month to stop deadheading in the UK. A local rose society is the place to ask.
statements.shown_to: Gardeners in the United Kingdom only

statements.question: Which months do I plant or move a rose?
statements.text: In the UK, plant a bare-root rose while it is dormant (not actively growing), between October and early March. Months are only a guide.
statements.shown_to: Gardeners in the United Kingdom only

statements.question: Which months do I plant or move a rose?
statements.text: Don't plant a bare-root rose while the ground is frozen. One rose grower says to keep it in a bucket of water or compost until the ground has thawed.
statements.shown_to: Gardeners in the United Kingdom only

statements.question: Which months do I plant or move a rose?
statements.text: A rose in a pot can be planted at any time of year, as long as the ground is not frozen, waterlogged or very dry. One garden company says the ideal months are September to November and March to May. Months are only a guide.
statements.shown_to: Gardeners in the United Kingdom only

statements.question: Which months do I plant or move a rose?
statements.text: One rose grower says not to plant a potted rose in extreme heat.
statements.shown_to: Gardeners in the United Kingdom only

statements.question: Which months do I plant or move a rose?
statements.text: Move an established rose while it is dormant, between November and February. For deciduous shrubs in general, one source says any time from late October to mid-March. Months are only a guide.
statements.shown_to: Gardeners in the United Kingdom only

statements.question: When do I clear up and spray in winter?
statements.text: Clear away fallen rose leaves in autumn, so that disease has nowhere to linger. One source says to destroy them, or bury them under a layer of mulch (material spread over the soil).
statements.shown_to: Gardeners in the United Kingdom only

statements.question: When do I clear up and spray in winter?
statements.text: One rose grower says to pick up fallen leaves and remove diseased ones in October and November, and to tidy the beds in February, ready for spring. Months are only a guide.
statements.shown_to: Gardeners in the United Kingdom only

statements.question: When do I clear up and spray in winter?
statements.text: One source says to pick off any leaves still on the rose over the winter months, if practical, and dispose of them.
statements.shown_to: Gardeners in the United Kingdom only

statements.question: When do I clear up and spray in winter?
statements.text: One rose grower says to check the base of your rose for exposed roots before the winter weather takes hold, and to build up a layer of mulch around any that show, to protect them from the cold.
statements.shown_to: Gardeners in the United Kingdom only

statements.question: When do I clear up and spray in winter?
statements.text: I couldn't find UK advice from a gardening body or rose society on spraying roses in winter. A local rose society is the place to ask.
statements.shown_to: Gardeners in the United Kingdom only

statements.question: When do I clear up and spray in winter?
statements.text: I couldn't find UK advice on mounding soil over the base of a rose for winter. A local rose society is the place to ask.
statements.shown_to: Gardeners in the United Kingdom only

statements.question: How do I allow for frost and my own garden?
statements.text: On average, the last frost of spring comes earlier in southern and coastal parts of the UK, often before the end of April, the national weather service says. Further north and on higher ground it often comes well into May, and in a few places in June. Late frosts still happen, so months are only a guide.
statements.shown_to: Gardeners in the United Kingdom only

statements.question: How do I allow for frost and my own garden?
statements.text: Frosts go on later in spring on an exposed, rural or high site than in a sheltered spot, in a town or near the coast. In a valley, cold air drains downhill and pools overnight, so frost is especially likely there.
statements.shown_to: Gardeners in the United Kingdom only

flags.sentence: Others say to wait until March in northern and colder areas.
flags.problem: 6: repeats UK item 2, which already says to wait until March in northern and colder areas.

flags.sentence: One of them says this is for tall roses, and that it is too early then for a hard prune.
flags.problem: 4: 'hard prune' is not explained anywhere in this answer.
flags.suggestion: Reword to say a hard prune (cutting the rose back firmly) is too early then, or say 'main prune'.

flags.sentence: Feed the rose again in mid-summer, after its first flush of flowers.
flags.problem: 4: 'flush' of flowers is not explained in this answer.
flags.suggestion: Reword as 'after its first round of flowers'.

flags.sentence: One rose grower says after the second flush of flowers.
flags.problem: 4: 'flush' is not explained in this answer.
flags.suggestion: Reword as 'after the second round of flowers'.

flags.sentence: I couldn't find a month to stop deadheading in the UK. A local rose society is the place to ask.
flags.problem: 6: contradicts items 1 and 2, which give months for stopping; confusing to see together.

flags.sentence: For deciduous shrubs in general, one source says any time from late October to mid-March.
flags.suggestion: Reword to 'For shrubs that lose their leaves in winter in general' or remove.

flags.sentence: One source says to pick off any leaves still on the rose over the winter months, if practical, and dispose of them.
flags.problem: 6: repeats item 1 (clear away leaves and destroy them) and item 2.

flags.sentence: I couldn't find UK advice from a gardening body or rose society on spraying roses in winter.
flags.problem: 1: talks about what the assistant could find, not about the rose or what to do; gives no action beyond asking.
flags.suggestion: Reword to 'Ask a local rose society about spraying roses in winter.'

flags.sentence: I couldn't find UK advice on mounding soil over the base of a rose for winter.
flags.problem: 1: about the search, not what the gardener does; 'mounding' is vague.
flags.suggestion: Reword to 'Ask a local rose society whether to mound soil over the base of the rose for winter.'

result.overall: Most statements are plain and actionable, with months and a clear action. The main problems are a few unexplained words (flush, hard prune, deciduous), the deadheading gap line that contradicts the months above it, and some repeated leaf-clearing and northern-March lines. The gap statements read as search reports rather than advice.
